records.name: Slovakia
records.summary:
Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveller-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues under the free-movement rules of the regional union this country belongs to, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022 a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside an LGBT bar in the capital — classified as the country's first modern terrorist attack. The national authorities responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital.

For a visitor: no legal exposure and functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against transgender recognition. The sources document no marriage or partner-recognition protections, so partner-based expectations should not be assumed.

sources.summary: Wikipedia timeline of the 12 October 2022 Bratislava shooting: a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger (the LGBT bar Teplaren was 'plan B') arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at Teplaren, killing two and injuring one. The article's investigation, victims and perpetrator sections document the planning, the LGBT-venue target and the aftermath.

Feature of 7 February 2023: Slovakia's trans community remains precarious after the 12 October 2022 terrorist attack on the Bratislava LGBT bar, which rights groups say 'marked a new era' for trans people in the country. Existing transition rules already required surgical sterilisation before changing documents, and the aftermath brought even greater fears about the future.
thin: no usable finding

Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović's letter (April 2023) to the Slovak National Council: six months after the Tepláreň attack, no discernible progress; human rights of LGBTI people appear more, not less, at risk; concerned about regressive legislative proposals including the LGR ban bill.
thin: no usable finding

records.name: Moldova
records.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Moldova: a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination, recommending preventive measures; hate speech remained serious with no meaningful state response (echoed in the European Commission country report); election-period political hate speech rose.

Amnesty International Moldova 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted (impunity for past violations); in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

GENDERDOC-M report (2023) citing the Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022" (published January 2023): acceptance of LGBT+ people is extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance 5.7), and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022.

Attitude (2 February 2026) revisiting Moldova Pride 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities — a country "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity"; public Pride proceeds openly.

ECOM legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV in Moldova (Tallinn, 2024): identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV — access to justice, hate-crime and discrimination provisions — based on a survey of local partners, benchmarked against international standards.

PinkNews (19 May 2018): police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters trying to disrupt the annual Moldova Pride solidarity march in Chisinau (19 May) as marchers carried foam hearts; activists feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes.

PinkNews (1 March 2013): the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the northern city’s "gay propaganda" ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights — local church-led bans struck down after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

records.name: Luxembourg
records.summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

sources.summary: Official Luxembourg government portal (Guichet.lu) page on applying to change one's gender status and first name(s) in the civil register - the administrative procedure for legal gender recognition.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; self-determination-based gender markers (no nonbinary markers); discrimination banned on sexual orientation and gender identity but not gender expression or sex characteristics; no measures on conversion practices or intersex interventions; in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, criticised by organisations for missing depathologisation and other key elements.

Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale UPR submission (April 2023) for Luxembourg: describes the organisation's services and Luxembourg's equality laws (employment, goods and services, education, health), the CET equality body and the national LGBTI action plan.

Asher Fergusson's LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index (updated June 2023): 400+ hours of research ranking all countries' laws for LGBTQ+ traveller safety, with a companion Global Transgender Rights Index - comparative data source covering Luxembourg.

Le Quotidien (June 2019, in French): 'Agressions LGBTphobes: un durcissement des sanctions attendu' - Luxembourg law lacks LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances; victims under-report; the justice minister signalled the law would evolve after ECRI's 2017 intervention.

Le Quotidien (May 2017, in French): Justice Minister Félix Braz presented a bill allowing trans and intersex people to change civil-status gender by declaration - replacing the long, costly judicial procedure; welcomed by associations.

Le Quotidien headline (July 2018) confirms the Chamber approved simplified civil-status change for trans people; body paywalled in fetched copy — vote split and procedure details unverifiable from the page itself.

records.name: Andorra
records.summary:
Andorra is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family modernised the legal framework (unified civil marriage, and legal gender recognition provisions); the Ministry of Equality now obliges all companies to maintain sexual and gender-based harassment protocols. ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

No traveler-facing concerns: no bathroom laws, no border issues (open border with Spain/France, though outside Schengen there are no document-gender checks), high social tolerance in practice despite a conservative Catholic history. Gaps: anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity is recent and shallower than Spain's; hate-crime law is generic rather than SOGI-specific. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Andorra chapter: a transphobic opinion piece in El Periòdic d'Andorra (27 Sep) was removed online with a public apology after DiversAnd's request though it had already run in print; in August DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for gender-affirming protocols — puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, in some cases 14 — following the 2022 regulatory changes.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025), Andorra chapter: Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month; DiversAnd flagged incidents during June Pride celebrations and called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence so it can be recognised as hate crime; the Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during the year.

PinkNews (Sep 12, 2023): Andorra's head of government Xavier Espot Zamora, in office since 2019, came out as gay publicly saying 'I never hid it' — a societal-climate signal for a country where he remains the serving prime minister.

GayLawNet Andorra laws page: age of consent is 16 under Penal Code Article 206, with topic coverage including civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status; marked 'limited information', useful as a dated legal-index pointer rather than analysis.
